points.requirement: An unchanged ligand can bind and be released reversibly; that does not itself depict chemical transformation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For a simple reversible binding equilibrium, Kd is the product of free partner concentrations divided by complex concentration; lower Kd means tighter binding under those conditions. Total added ligand need not equal free ligand. Affinity for one partner does not establish specificity against other partners.

Antagonism need not use the agonist’s binding site.

points.requirement: Separate estrogen/ER and progesterone/PR examples depict classical intracellular transcription regulation, not anER-PR complex.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An extracellular EGF ligand can change intracellular kinase signaling without entering the cell. Estrogen and progesterone bind their distinct intracellular receptors, which can regulate transcription with different forms and cellular partners. PD-1 engagement can restrain responding T-cell activity, so receptor activation is not always activation of tumor growth. FAP is a surface protease used as a targeting address, not a hormone/growth-factor receptor in this comparison.

points.requirement: The classical example does not mean all hormone effects require transcription, all genes increase or every receptor permanently resides in the nucleus.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Receptors can be on the surface or inside a cell. Ligand-gated ion channels regulate ion passage; G-protein-coupled receptors act through G proteins; enzyme-linked receptors can contain an enzyme or recruit a separate one. Intracellular nuclear receptors can regulate transcription with cellular partners. A surface signal can ultimately alter genes, while nuclear-receptor family membership does not fix every molecule permanently in the nucleus or require every effect to use new transcription.
